utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, may we have -- could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton; the case manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, for the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell; Liane Aronchick, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We are here today to hear the Defence's 98 bis submission, so who will take the floor? Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, indeed, it is me. Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom who have attended this trial from late in the autumn of last year. And it's our firm conviction, Your Honours, that on any sensible, reasonable, and correct view of the totality of the evidence that none of the 14 counts against Mr. Hadzic have been proven in respect of any of the events alleged against him over a two-and-a-half-year period between 1991 and 1993. But, Your Honours, your task at the 98 bis stage, and our task in attempting to assist you, is not to make submissions on a sensible, proper, or correct view of the totality of the evidence. Our only task and your only task is to assess whether there is any evidence upon which you could convict Mr. Hadzic of any of those crimes. And we propose today to focus our submissions accordingly, and those submissions will come in two parts, Mr. President: First, I propose to set out the law of 98 bis as best I understand it, and I will suggest to you in the course of those submissions that Your Honours are not bound by the four corners of the counts as articulated in the indictment in determining what portions of this case to allow to proceed. And I will show you that, in fact, there is jurisprudence showing that indeed Trial Chambers have gone within counts to examine whether or not there is a portion of a count that may be permitted to proceed. And I use the word "count" here advisably because what I suggest to you is meant by the word "count" in Rule 98 bis is not necessarily counts as defined by the Prosecution in the indictment. And I propose to set out for you the law and the logic behind that particular interpretation. And, Your Honours, after having presented that law, we will suggest that there are two areas in which counts should not be permitted to proceed in this case. And the first area is crimes alleged to have occurred in OG South. And the crimes alleged to have occurred in OG South are actually in four areas, as charged in the indictment: Lovas, Velepromet, Ovcara and Opatovac. And the second area where we suggest that charges should not be permitted to proceed is in respect of crimes in Serbia for which the Prosecution has not yet established that there is any application of international humanitarian law or crimes against humanity to that territory. So, Mr. President, let's now look at the text of Rule 98 bis: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision and after hearing the oral submissions of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." Now, Mr. President, it's often been said in the jurisprudence and I think it's obvious for those of us who has similar provisions in our domestic systems that this is an efficiency mechanism designed to allow Your Honours to remove charges when there is no real prospect of success on those charges, and the efficiency aspect of that is that alleviates the Defence of the need to call evidence in response to charges even if it's believed that there is no evidence upon which a conviction could be sustained; nevertheless, the Defence often will call such evidence out of an abundance of caution. And the 98 bis procedure allows Your Honours to examine the evidence and determine whether or not there is such a need. And secondly, it allows Your Honours to, even if no evidence is called by the Defence in respect of that particular charge, to eliminate it at this stage summarily because it simply has no merit. And the first aspect of Rule 98 bis is that the 98 bis standard of no evidence capable of supporting a conviction applies to each element of the alleged crime. It applies to each element of the alleged crime. There must be some evidence capable of supporting a conviction which means that there must be some evidence upon which Your Honours could find beyond a reasonable doubt the existence of each element of the alleged crime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You are kindly asked to slow down for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, just while there is the brief pausing, my deepest apologies to counsel, in the record which has moved past us now on the screen, the court reporter did didn't get the location of the fourth place where counsel had indicated the case should not move forward, and I would appreciate if he could just indicate. He had said the four places in OG South: Lovas, Velepromet, Opatovac, and what was the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It was Ovcara, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now according to the Jelesic Appeals Chamber, which is a decision from 2001, the test under 98 bis is whether there is evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonably Tribunal of fact could convict; that is to say, evidence, if accepted, upon which a reasonable Tribunal of fact could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused on the particular charge in question. Now, this is actually the language that is the precursor to what is now the language in Rule 98 bis, as it was amended in 2004. And I say that because the key element is whether or not Your Honours could, not "will," could convict beyond a reasonable doubt. And if we go to the next slide, sometimes it's said simply that there must be no evidence at all in respect of an element of a crime in order to satisfy the 98 bis standard, but that's not quite correct, Mr. President, I would suggest. There must be no evidence supporting of a particular count, that's one option; or, and this is from the Mrksic case, if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution. And then we see a slight variation on that from the Prlic Trial Chamber: When there is no evidence of sustaining a conviction, that's one option; or when there is evidence but even when taken at its highest this evidence could not sustain a conviction by the Trial Chamber; or when the only evidence available is clearly unreliable or incapable of belief. Now we say that that last statement is the most comprehensive and correct articulation of the 98 bis standard, and that Your Honours should not feel yourselves bound by some kind of cliometric analysis of whether there happens to be a data point inside of a box in which crimes are measured against modes of liability. Your Honours are permitted, even if you're not going to go so far as to examine a correct, sensible, or proper view of the totality of the evidence, you do have the discretion, and I suggest that it is appropriate for you to exercise that discretion, if you see the evidence now is not evidence upon which at the end of the case you could rely. If you know that now, then you are permitted to discard that, and you are permitted now to say that that is not a sufficient basis upon which charges may be permitted to continue. And there will be occasions when that is the case, Mr. President. There will be occasions, and we -- our submissions will reflect this. There are occasions where evidence was heard in this court or where there is a line from a document which may fall within the box of being probative of one of the charges that we say should not be permitted to continue, but Your Honours should not be bound to accept any level of evidence that may have come before you. You may look at the evidence and decide that it is not a basis upon which you will be able to enter a conviction. And we say that that is perfectly within the spirit of Rule 98 bis. In fact, it would be contrary to the spirit of Rule 98 bis if you were bound to allow charges to proceed whenever there is some evidence, no matter how unreliable, no matter how tenuous in respect of the fact that needs to be established, to say that that would be a sufficient basis to proceed and that you would not have a discretion, because that's what we are talking about here, a discretion to consider whether or not the charges may not be allowed to proceed. Now, how does this threshold apply in respect of a circumstantial case? Because this is not an issue that has actually been analysed to any significant degree in previous case law. It's one thing to say, Your Honours, that in respect of the judgement of acquittal standard where you have direct evidence, that as long as there is one item of direct evidence that is probative of the fact that needs to be proven, that's sufficient to proceed. That's one case. But isn't it another case, Your Honours, when you're dealing with circumstantial evidence where, after all, almost anything can be circumstantially probative of anything else. The mere fact that Mr. Hadzic is present in eastern Croatia can be invoked by the Prosecution as circumstantially probative of various aspects of its case, and surely it's not sensible to suggest that that is a sufficient basis far a charge to proceed. But let's look at what is required of a circumstantial case at the end of the day. The standard is that: "A Trial Chamber may infer the existence of a particular fact upon which the guilt of the accused depends from circumstantial evidence only if it is the only reasonable conclusion that could be drawn from the evidence presented. If there is another conclusion, which is also reasonably open from the evidence and which is consistent with the nonexistence of that fact, the conclusion of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt cannot be drawn." So the standard, Mr. President, is, in my respectful view, when applied to a circumstantial case, is whether there is evidence capable of excluding reasonable inferences inconsistent with the particular fact required to be established. Now the quotation has just disappeared from the screen, but it's down there at the last bullet. And, Mr. President, I don't want there to be any confusion about this. That's my submission. That's my crystallisation, I would suggest, of the law. In respect of direct evidence, yes, a single piece of evidence is sufficient to allow a case to proceed if you think it is sufficient, if it is capable of proving the required element. Circumstantial evidence, that's not the case. It's not the case because it would be absurd. It would mean that any disparate, tenuously connected fact to the element that needs to be proved would be sufficient to allow the case to proceed. And that makes no sense. And what we suggest, Mr. President, again, and perhaps that is an ode to discretion, you have the discretion to examine whether or not there is a conjunction of evidence upon which, yes, on a summary review, a cursory review, you can say to yourselves: All of these facts in conjunction might lead us to conclude that the element exists. And that is the inquiry, I suggest, that is before you at the 98 bis stage. Now there is some evidence, I suggest, that Your Honours intrinsically should and can at the 98 bis stage discard as not evidence upon which you will be able to rely at the end of the day. And the first category of such evidence which is well-established in the 98 jurisprudence is "incapable of belief." It's a broad category, a broad definition, and it reflects, I suggest again, the discretion that Trial Chambers have in assessing the evidence that's been brought before them. I would hazard two additional categories that I think fall within the definition of incapable of belief, although I must say I'm not entirely sure that incapable of belief captures the totality of Your Honours analysis, and I would refer you back to the Prlic Trial Chamber's description which was that there be evidence upon which -- evidence which is clearly unreliable or incapable of belief. And evidence that is clearly unreliable, includes, I would suggest, Your Honours, evidence that is based on anonymous sources. It's well-established in international human rights law and in many national systems that a conviction cannot be based on an anonymous source. In fact, I would go further and say that an anonymous source, unless there are very, very stringent guarantees, procedural or substantive, can be accorded no weight whatsoever. And Your Honours have heard some evidence in this courtroom that was based on anonymous sources, upon which and in respect of which the Defence has no opportunity at all to test. And I would suggest that it's well-established that Your Honours will not be able to rely on that at the end of the day, knowing that that's the case as a matter of law that at the end of the day, you cannot rely on anonymous sources, I suggest, that it follows that halfway through the day you have the discretion to consider such evidence to be manifestly unreliable and not capable of sustaining proof of an element of a crime. And the third area where I would say it's well-established that evidence is not reliable to prove an element of a crime is where you have uncorroborated hearsay. And the way that this is usually formulated in the case law, in judgements is that decisive weight cannot be placed on hearsay. So, Your Honours, I would suggest again that if we have an occasion, if you see that there is evidence that is hearsay, fully understand that that is not categorically inadmissible, fully understand that hearsay can be part of the broader mix of evidence, perfectly appropriate to consider it within broader context of circumstantial evidence, that's all permissible. And if Your Honours are in doubt on a cursory review of the evidence about the issue, then, of course, you can rely on hearsay evidence. But if you're in a situation where you see that there is a fact that depends solely on one piece of hearsay evidence, then Your Honours have a discretion to determine that that is not evidence upon which you could sustain a finding of the existence of an element of a crime. Now those submissions were all directed towards the issue of whether there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction, those last six words of Rule 98 bis. And now I want to focus on the parameters of your analysis and whether or not you are required to consider this issue only in respect of the counts as defined in the indictment presented to you by the Prosecution. And let's really understand what's at stake here in practical terms. The Prosecution is permitted to produce an indictment, submit it to a single Judge ex parte. That indictment is either then confirmed or rejected by a single Judge. Based on my understanding, Judges - and there is no criticism of this whatsoever - who are involved in the process of confirming indictments do not require the Prosecution to put the indictment in any particular form. Basically, it's the Prosecution's discretion to devise an indictment in whatever form it wishes. And this is different from some systems of law, of course, where an indictment is prepared by a judicial official based upon information provided by a prosecutor, or where a judicial official has a significant role in ensuring that the indictment is structured in a proper manner. And when I say proper manner, I mean a manner that accords by whatever guidelines, rules, that are set out by the code of criminal procedure in that system. And of course, we don't have that here at the ICTY, and I'm not criticising, but what I am saying is that there is a -- this is a system which must be considered as a whole, and I would suggest that there is a relationship between the extent of discretion accorded to the Prosecution in structuring its indictments and the extent of discretion that Your Honours should give yourselves at the 98 bis stage in examining the parameters against which you determine whether there is evidence that should proceed. And I'll start with a couple of examples to show how the Prosecution exercises this discretion and how significant it is in understanding how Rule 98 bis functions from case to case. Now this, Your Honours, is an extract from the Lukic indictment. And all the counts in the Lukic indictment are structured the same as this count that I'm presenting to you on the screen. And what we see in this -- in these counts is that the crimes -- the counts are indeed crimes: Count 6 is murder and count 7 is murder. So a count is defined as a crime. And I can tell you that elsewhere in this indictment, there are other counts that also charge murder. So again, the count is defined as a crime. But look at how the counts are defined in relation to the charges or allegations. They are confined to a specific event. And that means that at the 98 bis stage the Trial Chamber is analysing whether there is sufficient evidence upon which it could conclude that the accused are guilty of this event and equally in respect of the other events. The Prosecution could just as well, assuming that it were to follow the format of this indictment, have had a long list of paragraphs in which it said, Here is incident one, incident two, incident three, incident four, incident five, incident six, and then at the end charged crime, the crime of murder, as a count. At least that's what its purports to do. And there is no one to say otherwise, Mr. President. And that links back to what I was saying earlier. The judges who are examining these issues, I would suggest, are no instructing, at least as far as I know, that indictments be restructured. And yet I would suggest that this is a considerably fairer indictment than the one that has been alleged against Mr. Hadzic. I don't say that the indictment against Mr. Hadzic fails against the standards of the forms of pleading that have been set out by this Tribunal. Your Honours have already ruled on that and I'm not suggesting otherwise. What I am suggesting, however, again, is that there is a relationship between the discretion that you have and should exercise at the 98 bis stage and the manner in which an indictment has been structured and pleaded. Let's look at another example, one with which I believe at least two of Your Honours are familiar. And this is the Haradinaj indictment. And again, this was an indictment that was structured throughout in the same way as in respect of the counts you see on the screen in front of you. And we see crimes charged -- counts charged as crimes or crimes charged as counts in respect of individual events, and the entire indictment is structured in the same way. Now, how does Black's Law Dictionary define a count? And again, we're talking about the use of the word in Rule 98 bis. That's why I'm making these submissions about counts because it has to do with what we say is the proper interpretation of that word in Rule 98 bis. Black's Law Dictionary says that a account is: "The different parts of a declaration, each of which, if it stood alone, would constitute a ground for action, are the counts of the declaration. Used also to signify the several parts of an indictment, each charging a distinct offence." Now it's one thing to charge genocide and encompass a wide array of distinct events, because the pattern, as the law suggests, can be relevant to proving the elements of genocide. The same is not true, Mr. President, in respect of a crime like murder, which is sustainable in respect of a single killing, as long as the elements are proven. Equally, even in respect of extermination, there is case law about the extent to which disparate events can be strung together in order to sustain a charge of extermination. And the bottom line on that jurisprudence, as I understand it, is that there is a limit to which you can string together disparate events in order to attempt to show that there has been a collective killing that establishes the requisite threshold for extermination. And I would suggest that the disparate elements that you see -- the disparate killings that you see in the indictment against Mr. Hadzic go far beyond the extent that is permitted for determining a collective killing event under extermination. So what I'm suggesting to Your Honours, quite simply, is that there is no reason and no justification for not having charged separate killing events as separate counts, as was done in the Haradinaj and the Lukic indictments, and I would suggest that that would be a proper definition of the word "count." Of course, the indictment against Mr. Hadzic says otherwise. Of course it's not defined that way or structured that way because the Prosecution is not necessarily going to structure its indictments in a manner that is the most convenient or helpful for the Defence, and nor is a Judge confirming an indictment necessarily going to be inclined to intervene on such a matter at such a stage without hearing submissions from the other side. Perfectly reasonable that that would be the case. And here at the 98 bis stage, leaving aside pleading defects - we're not saying it's a pleading defect - we're saying it's -- pleading that is not optimally fair, which is a different thing. But leaving aside pleading defects, 98 bis is the first occasion that Your Honours have to take a look at how you are going to interpret and address an indictment in relation to the evidence heard. And again, I'm suggesting that these are reasons, this structure, this context, these are all reasons why you can go towards not the counts in form but the counts in substance. And that's what I would suggest is meant by Rule 98 bis. And let's look precisely at how the wording of Rule 98 bis changed in this regard in 2004. And I would suggest, unfortunately, that the word change doesn't actually tell us very much about the issue before us. The old wording of Rule 98 bis was: "The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of judgement of acquittal on motion of an accused or proprio motu if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges." But the problem wasn't so much with the wording, the old wording of Rule 98 bis, it was rather that there was a divergence of practice as to how Rule 98 bis should be applied before 2004. Because in some 98 bis decisions, the Chambers evaluated on a paragraph by paragraph basis whether or not the allegations had been proven, even if all of those individual paragraphs were connected with, what I would say, is even a single count in substantive terms. So they were looking at material facts, Mr. President. And you can imagine how laborious that was, particularly when the parties are allowed to offer written submissions. And that's why in some cases, such as the Milosevic case, the 98 bis judgement was in itself a mini judgement. And this was certainly not in the interests of efficiency. And Judge Robinson, at the end of that lengthy judgement, I would suggest, quite correctly criticised the extent to which 98 bis had been hijacked and sent down the road of an analysis of material facts. And what he says as an antidote or offers as an antidote to this is he says that: "Consideration should be given to confining motions under Rule 98 bis to submissions that are designed to eliminate a charge or count rather than individual allegations of fact relating thereto." So the distinction that's identified here by Judge Robinson is not between charges and counts. He views them, at least in this particular sentence, as equivalent. The issue is between counts or charges and material facts. And Judge Robinson is saying that material facts are not an appropriate reference point for considering whether or not the 98 bis threshold is satisfied. Now, of course, at the end of this year, in 2004, Rule 98 bis was amended. And as I understand it, Judge Robinson's opinions were very relevant to that amendment. And if we turn and look at one other indication of legislative intent, if I can put it that way, because I suggest that Judge Robinson's separate opinion is an indication of legislative intent in respect of Rule 98 bis, and we have another indication of legislative intent in respect of 98 bis, and this comes from Judge Antonetti in the Seselj case. And here he is in dissent, and he says: "The majority opinion is that it is not possible to enter a judgement of partial acquittal based on the wording of this Rule. I disagree totally with their interpretation, all the more so since I'm the co-author, together with another Judge, of the very wording of the new Rule. The purpose of this reform was never to make it impossible to enter a decision of partial acquittal. It would have been paradoxical that the very purpose of this reform, which is to gain time, actually would have reached the opposite result on the very ground that it is not possible to enter a decision of partial acquittal. It would be equally paradoxical to force the accused to adduce evidence whilst for specific counts or parts of counts the Prosecutor did not lead any evidence or because the evidence they have adduced is not sufficient." And then he goes on to suggest that there may be an issue of interpretation arising from the two equally authoritative languages. Now what I understand Judge Antonetti to be referring to when he says "partial acquittal," and I think it's clear when you read it in context, he's referring to partial acquittal within an count, within an individual count. Now, if you would not adopt this interpretation, if Your Honours reject this interpretation, what are the practical consequences of that? It means, and we can, in fact, take a look at our indictment, in -- for example, in respect of count 3, murder, which is preceded by a whole long list of individual events and killing. It would mean that even if there are 25, 30, 40 individual killing events pled in the indictment over the course of years in entirely different geographic locations, committed by totally different perpetrators with no apparent connection to one another, totally distinction, disparate events, if you don't accept Judge Antonetti's views on this, it would mean that if any one of those, let's say hypothetically 50 - it's not that many here in our indictment, but it's a couple of dozen - if any one of those has some evidence on which Your Honour's could convict, it means that they all have to proceed? Your Honours don't have a discretion to consider whether those events are interrelated? Your Honours don't have a discretion to consider whether some of them may fall within a discrete time-frame or a discrete geographic location? Your Honours don't have a discretion to decide that that particular discrete identifiable portion should not be permitted to go forward, even though the consequence of that would be that evidence then needs to be called on all of the charges, even if there is no evidence. And I use the word "charges" here as an equivalent to counts because I say that there is a difference between counts in substance and contents in form. And when you have an individual charge that is sufficient in itself to constitute a crime, that's a count, even if the Prosecution's indictment is not structured that way. And the efficiency consequences of not accepting Judge Antonetti's view, I suggest, run directly contrary to the purpose of Rule 98 bis, that is suggested there quite directly by Judge Antonetti and more obliquely by Judge Robinson. And by the way, Judge Robinson himself, as far as I know, has never had occasion to comment on this issue judicially because in Lukic you had an indictment that was structured according to events. Counts corresponding to events. Is there practice to support what I'm saying as opposed to just judicial statements or concurring opinions? In the Stanisic and Simatovic case, you have very broad counts, counts that encompass a geographic spread and a temporal spread of events that is even broader than in this case. Now, in the result the Trial Chamber, after hearing submissions only from one of the Defence teams, the Simatovic team, allowed the entire case to go forward. Nothing was rejected. But that was on a review of the evidence provided. And how did it review the evidence provided? Well, Your Honours, it reviewed the evidence provided according to its own analysis of what it considered to be geographically and temporally connected, which, by the way, was in the indictment itself, just not defined as separate counts. And so the Chamber proceeded to analyse the sufficiency of the evidence under Rule 98 bis according to each of the three main geographic areas in respect of the charges. So it analysed the sufficiency of the evidence in the SAO Krajina, in the SAO SBWS, and in Bosnia separately. It examined each of the counts in respect of each of those geographic regions. Similarly in Karadzic, the Trial Chamber examined components, so-called components of the case which, again, had no formal definition in the indictment other than to examine and review the indictment and identify which areas, geographically or temporally, should be connected, and the evidence was also presented according to those components. And Their Honours in the Karadzic case separately analysed each of those areas. Now, if it simply had been a manner of counts -- and by the way, we shouldn't confuse the issue in the Karadzic case, count 1, genocide in respect of certain areas of Bosnia as distinct from count 2, genocide in Srebrenica. Of course the Chamber analysed those two counts separately. I'm not discussing that issue. This is a separate question of whether the other charges, which were not broken out geographically, whether those could be analysed separately. And that's what the Trial Chamber did. If it had just been a question of saying, Well, is there some evidence on the count in respect of any of the geographic areas, then the Chamber wouldn't have had to analyse or structure its analysis according to this geographic and temporal definition. So what do we have in totality? What can we draw from this practice and these statements? I suggest there are two principles that emerge from the case law: The first is that Your Honours do have a discretion to go beyond the counts as defined by the Prosecution. That's clear from these examples and it's strongly supported by the statements made by at least two Judges. And I would suggest that it is perfectly concordant and appropriate in light of the purpose of Rule of 98 bis. And then the question is: If that's true, how should Your Honours exercise that discretion. How should you define the reference point of your analysis? And I would say that is a matter essentially for your sound discretion. And I would say you should guide your discretion according to whether or not there are groups of events that you can identify as significantly discrete, separate, distinct events that should be analysed as such. And that's what I invite you to do in respect of our substantive submissions and the specific areas that we invite you to take a look at. And so now having set out, I suggest, the proper framework for Rule 98 bis at this stage, we make our substantive submissions on those counts that we suggest should not proceed. And we suggest that counts 2 to 9 -- we submit that counts 2 to 9 should not be permitted to proceed according to the standards of Rule 98 bis in respect of events in OG South. And the four events and the relevant portions of the indictment are: Lovas, paragraph 18 of the indictment; Velepromet on the 19th of November; the events of Ovcara on the 20th of November; and Opatovac. And we also suggest that there is no sufficient basis for the case to proceed in respect of any and all crimes in Serbia. And that's mainly counts 7 to 9. Now it might be helpful before reviewing the evidence to give a thumbnail sketch, by no means an exhaustive sketch, a thumbnail sketch of the cardinal elements of liability that would need to be established in order to find Mr. Hadzic guilty. And at this stage, again, it's not a question of whether or not the evidence on a correct view establishes that to be the case, but whether there is some evidence, some reliable evidence, upon which you could come to that view. And what I have done on this single slide is to attempt to crystalise, as I say extremely briefly, the various modes of liability upon which Mr. Hadzic could be found criminally responsible. The first bullet point reflects JCE 1, and for that matter direct commission as a whole; the second bullet point is JCE 3; the third is aiding and abetting; and the fourth is superior responsibility. It's important to remember that, and I'm sure Your Honours don't need to be reminded of this, that JCE is a form of direct participation. The intent required, the mens rea to find that a person is participating in a JCE, is precisely the same mens rea as is required if a person commits a crime on his or her own. It's the same as if a person swings a machete and commits a violent act against a victim. That is the mens rea threshold. The unique aspect of JCE as a form of direct commission is not in respect of the mens rea but in respect of the actus reus which is diffused amongst different individuals. But that notwithstanding that same dolus directus that applies in respect of an individual committing a crime on his own or her own applies in respect of JCE, and that makes your task difficult, Mr. President, because in respect of an individual swinging a machete it's rather easy in almost all circumstances to draw the necessary inferences about mens rea. In respect of an individual alleged to be participating in a common plan, a common criminal plan, the necessary mens rea inference is a lot more fraught and complicated. But that mens rea standard is still there. It's not less because the allegations that the crime is committed through others. And Your Honours know that the case law says that these others and this enterprise can be quite broad. There is no necessary restriction on its scope, which again makes your task all the harder, especially where, as here, we have such a broadly charged JCE. What's more, and I say this is absolutely vital not only for understanding the actus reus of JCE but also for understanding whether and how Your Honours can draw the necessary inferences of mens rea, is that the crime must be committed by other members of that common plan, of that JCE, or it must be committed by individuals who are controlled by other members of the JCE. And that comes from the Brdjanin appeals judgement. Now it's very common, and Your Honours have seen this in previous cases and there is no dispute about it, that organisational structures can be a way through which these modes of liability are effectuated and upon which inferences can be drawn about the necessary mens rea and about whether or not a contribution was made to the crime. But if an organisational structure is going to be relied upon to establish those elements, and we say that this is -- we're clearly in the realm of a circumstantial case here, then that organisational structure has to exist, and there has to be sufficient evidence for Your Honours to say that the organisational structure encompasses the crimes that are alleged against Mr. Hadzic, and if the evidence is not sufficient to establish that, then there is no liability, certainly on JCE grounds. And so Your Honours inquiry, I suggest at this stage, is: Is there evidence upon which you might be capable of determining that there was an organisational structure involving Mr. Hadzic that also encompassed the crimes that were committed in OG South. Because that's the question that we're bringing before you at this stage. And I should add that what I'm about to say about OG South applies elsewhere, but we consider that the evidence is very clear - and I should say the lack of evidence is very clear - about the lack of an organisational structure connecting Mr. Hadzic to any of the crimes that were alleged to have occurred in OG South. Equally in respect of aiding and abetting and superior responsibility, these can be shown and effectuated through an organisational structure. But there, the level of organisational structure, if anything, has to be even more distinct. There has to be some indication of specific direction of assistance to the crime. And that's always the connection, Your Honours. That's always the connection. The connection between the accused and his actions and the crime. And in respect of aiding and abetting, the question is whether his actions were specifically directed towards the crime and whether they made a substantial contribution to the crime. And then, of course, in respect of superior responsibility, I'd suggest the cardinal element, and the only one that I need to invoke at this stage is effective control, which implies a high level of connection, a high level of relationship, a relationship of subordination, obedience to orders between the perpetrator of the crime and the accused. So what is OG South? Now, we say that OG South existed certainly no later than the end of September through, at the very least, the 24th of November. We say that beyond that in one form or another. But it doesn't matter because one thing is clear, and I don't think it will be disputed, is that OG South exists at the times that each of the four crimes that we are saying there is no evidence to proceed on occurred. If we can go to the next slide, Your Honours will remember this map which was shown more than once. And it indicates on the map where OG South was located. And OG South existed firstly as a matter of military creation by the JNA. They created OG South. And they created a hierarchy within OG south. And that hierarchy and organisation was reflective of reality on the ground; namely, that there was a physical separation between the area south of Vukovar and the area north of Vukovar in the sense that there were Croat forces in between up until a certain date. But even when that corridor to Vukovar had been eliminated, OG South continued to exist. Now what is the scope and extent of that organisational structure that was set up by the JNA? Well, very helpfully, and I commend the Prosecution for calling this witness, we heard from the person who was the head of what he described as the TO staff for OG South. And he was appointed in October 1991. He testified that he was "subordinated to the commander of OG South, Mr. Mrksic," throughout his tenure. The second commander, Vujovic, was appointed by Sljivancanin or Mrksic immediately before the fall of Vukovar. The headquarters of the TO staff of OG South was in Velepromet. And he was asked by my learned colleague -- actually, I have to retract that, I'm not sure whether it was a question by the Prosecution or the Defence, but he was asked: "Roughly how many village TO staffs were subordinate to you? "A. There were more than 20 villages and all the units that were there, including Petrova Gora." Now, that's the evidence of someone who really was in a position to know, and who, by the way, there is no suggestion that I've heard from the Prosecution or during its questioning, was biased or in any way inclined towards Mr. Hadzic. Now what is the evidence taken at its highest? Taken at its highest, what is the evidence showing that this witness, GH-012, who had connections -- who was the commander, by his own account, the commander of the TO staff of OG South, which encompasses at least 20 villages in OG South, which at this time is physically separated from OG North, at least in Croatia. Now what is evidence, taken at its highest, of his connection with anyone in the district government, let alone Mr. Hadzic? Well, he explains that he met at one stage, and I believe it is in September because this is in reference to whether or not he and his forces should join up with the JNA forces in an attempt to liberate the Vukovar barracks. So that's the context of the first quotation. So GH-012 says -- and by the way, Your Honours, you will remember that at least according to this witness that that occurred in September, at least the initial liberation. And GH- 012 says that he met with Ilija Kojic who he believed and described as being the head of the Borovo Selo TO, which he described as "more organised" in order to "get to the corps command through him." Then they go together to see General Bratic in Novi Sad. Now, by the way, if I recall correctly, this is before GH- 012 is appointed to be the head of OG South, and that's why they are going to see General Bratic who, as you know, is not actually in the OG South formation, but that's because this is occurring before the formation of OG south.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at this stage, September 1991, GH-012 makes no mention of the district government. He doesn't appear to suggest that it exists. He mentions no affiliation of Mr. Kojic with the district government. No indication that the district government is providing or -- any assistance or able to provide any such assistance. The entire encounter with Mr. Kojic is vis-à-vis his role as the leader of the TO of Borovo Selo in order to get in touch with General Bratic who, in turn, this witness expects to get in touch with the local JNA commander in his area around Vukovar. So that's the first indication, and I suggest that even taken at its highest, it shows no connection - organisational, ad hoc, or otherwise - between the district government and OG South. Now here's the witness talking about him being appointed, and Colonel Mrksic apparently putting some kind of restriction on him, and I put the entire quotation in here because I think the context is important and because I expected the Prosecution in due course to perhaps point out this particular section and I wanted to put it all in context. And GH-012 says: "I was appointed TO Staff Commander, but I could not discharge solely that duty. Mrksic did not allow for that because then the Petrova Gora unit would be without a leader." Now let me stop there and indicate what I think the witness is saying. He's saying that Mrksic is complaining about the witness double-hatting, being at one and the same time the commander of TO of OG South and the commander of the Petrova Gora TO: "He said that it was important for us to liberate Vukovar and that the commander of TO staff was a political function and that we should now focus on the liberation of Vukovar. Consequently, I had to stay with the Petrova Gora unit until the liberation. "Q. In what way is the TO Staff Commander a political function? "A. It was a political function because, let's say, the TO finances, equips, and appoints municipal TO commanders. So it's not a military structure; it's a municipal/civilian structure. "Q. And do TO staffs fall under a government institution; and, if so, which institution? "A. They fall under the Ministry of Defence." Now, what exactly is Witness GH-012 saying here? What does he mean when he says -- when he was asked the question: "And do TO staffs fall under a government institution?" Because that was the question. The question wasn't were you at the time under a particular government institution. It was a general question about TO staffs in general. Based on what? We don't know. But I suggest from the entire context, that what the witness is saying is that Mrksic, based on his understanding of how TO staffs usually function, i.e., in peacetime and before the conflict, it is the case that local TO staffs do have an organisational connection with political authorities. Not operational, Mr. President. Not an operational connection and not a command and control connection. And that was made clear by Witness Theunens. This discussion is an abstract discussion about the general situation of TO staffs. Not the situation that he may -- felt he had with the district government of the SBWS. And it's not even clear from this statement, Mr. President, and it's a salient question to ask, which ministry of defence was he referring to. Was he referring to the SFRY? Was he referring to the government of Serbia? None of that was clarified in this question and answer. And, Mr. President, this was a question that was asked during direct examination of the witness. Then during cross-examination, the witness stated clearly the quotation from the previous slide, which was that he was subordinated throughout his tenure to Mrksic. And there was no follow-up by the Prosecution. They did not ask for a clarification. They did not say, But, Mr. Witness, you said during your direct examination that somehow you had some responsibilities vis-à-vis the Ministry of Defence. What about that? Those questions were not asked. The question was just left to stand, and I suggest that the question on cross-examination is the one that provides clarity and context for this statement. So we say that taken at its highest, at its absolute highest, and this is from the key witness, Mr. President, taken at its highest this shows no organisational connection between the district government and the TOs in OG South. And let's look at one other aspect of the evidence which helps understand all this. Because, Mr. President, I realise I may be labouring to describe the evidence to you, and it may be as paradoxical to you, why would I, in order to show that there is no evidence, be discussing the evidence to such a degree? And that would be a fair question to ask. And I do so because I think that there is a great deal of evidence in this case that can be taken completely out of context and that can be urged upon you as probative of an element of the crimes charged or as establishing the modes of liability but which, in fact, show no such thing at all. And what I'm trying to do, Your Honours, is to put that in context, to show you that that's the case in respect of many items of evidence that can be taken from here and there and presented to you and say, Oh, well, here, look at this connection. But I suggest, Mr. President, that it's not capable of sustaining a conviction on these particular -- in respect of these particular events. And let's put this -- let's discuss context. Because here is one document that's in evidence, it's an exhibit, that could be cited to say, Oh, look, look at the connection between OG South and the district government. And this was the town commander of Ilok writing in December 1991. And he says -- granted, this is late in the day, relative to the crime events that we're describing, Mr. President, but it's not atypical of the kind of material that can be found in the documents, and -- which I suggest is largely highly ambiguous. And what Colonel Belic says is, in a letter to Mr. Hadzic, so it's an important document: "As you are not contesting the presence of the army in this area," and this is around Ilok, and by the way there was evidence that Belic was the commander not just of Ilok but he was responsible for several villages in that area, "this leads to the conclusion that the army is there not because it is a zone of combat activity and because it is carrying out combat tasks but because you are graciously allowing it to be there." Now, one of the Prosecution experts, Dr. Nielsen, was asked about this passage in cross-examination, and what he said, I think, Mr. President, is highly significant. He said: "Well, it's -- it's -- to me it's a puzzling statement, not least because he then goes on to state that everyone knows that the army arrived before the authorities of the Serb district. So I have no idea whether he is trying to sound facetious or not, but it is certainly the case that the army arrived in many cases before the district authorities, and this term of 'graciously permitting us to be there,' again, to me, it simply sounds facetious." Now, I suggest that even on a cursory view of what there is referred to as 65 ter 6059, but I do now it's also a Prosecution exhibit or a Defence exhibit, even on a cursory view of that document, it's clear that it's not evidence capable of sustaining the view that the district government is in any position of authority, first of all of the JNA, and secondly of the TO staffs, the local TO staffs, and also the OG South TO staff, in that area. It doesn't prove that. And Nielsen, who I believe in this respect is absolutely correct and reliable, not only shows and indicates that that's not true, not only is it not evidence of that, it's evidence of the exact contrary. This is a mere colonel, JNA colonel, essentially mocking the president of the district government, being facetious towards him. And we say that that is a violate context, at least for understanding this particular piece of documentary evidence. It's not what it appears to be at face value even on a cursory view, Mr. President. Another example of that, Mr. President, is --

There is no evidence that that occurred at all. So that being the case, that there is no evidence of that having occurred, then the statement doesn't show authority. It doesn't show an organisational control over events in OG South in any degree. Those prisoners were all in the custody of JNA throughout the time that they were arrested, detained, marshalled in various locations including Velepromet, the Vukovar barracks, and the Vukovar hospital, and then taken either to Serbia or, for some unfortunate ones, Ovcara. And that all occurred in the custody of the JNA, as I'm going to discuss further. The point is that video does not show any organisational connection between what is going on in OG South and the district government, let alone a connection to Mr. Hadzic himself either -- and this is where we come back to the modes of liability, either that he is controlling events to a degree sufficient for Your Honours to conclude that crimes being committed in OG South are with his knowledge, that he intends those crimes, or that he is making a substantial contribution to the crimes. To say nothing, that he is -- would be alleged to be specifically directing assistance to those crimes. The organisational connection, again, often relied upon as the basis for these modes of liability, it's absent. There is not basis to sustain a conviction on that ground. Now, Mr. President, if it's convenient, can we perhaps take the break now?
