utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now let's look at the individual villages in OG South, at least OG South as it was defined by GH-012, and the allegations and the counts in respect of each of those villages. At paragraph 21 -- or, excuse me, indictment paragraph 26, which relates to counts 2, 3, and 4, and then paragraph 41(m), relates to counts 5 through 9. And let's go to the next slide, please. Now, what was the evidence about who was responsible? Well, let me put it a different way: Who directly perpetrated the crimes in Lovas? Well, the main evidence was that Ljuban Devetak, Milan Radojcic, and the Dusan Silni Detachment were involved in the crimes that occurred in Lovas village, and that included the minefield incident about which I'm sure Your Honours recalled the testimony. But what was said in the evidence about who is there, who is actually controlling these events? Who is organising them, who possesses authority, what organisational structure is there? Well, GH-102 indicated at P50, Exhibit P50, paragraph 152: "It is difficult to know how many JNA soldiers were deployed in Lovas, but I noticed that they controlled everything." P296, which is from GH-134, paragraph 6: "Radojcic ... as far as I was aware his uniform was regular JNA and not reservist. There were three stars on his epaulettes." And then I suggest that this was a vital concession by the Prosecution expert, military expert. And I see embedded in this quotation there is a reference to P378, Exhibit P378, upon which Mr. Theunens comment at transcript page 4572, and at the beginning there is a quotation which is read to Mr. Theunens, which reads: "'Civilian authorities have not been established to date in the town of Ilok or the villages of Sarengrad, Mohovo, Opatovac, Lovas, and Bapska ...'" And then the question: "Q. Let's just stop there. Assuming that that pronouncement -- well, whether that pronouncement is correct or not, the consequence of his statement," and this is Colonel Milan Belic, writing on the 9th of December, 1991, "that there are no local authorities is that the town command still exercises civilian control over those towns, right? "A. Yes. Actually, that the town command -- the military town commander is still responsible for conducting civil affairs in these towns." Now let's go to the next page and try to look at the evidence at its highest about Mr. Hadzic's connection to these events. And let's bear in mind, Your Honours, that it's not simply sufficient to say, Well, these are the same crimes being committed elsewhere in SBWS. That's not enough. Because as Brdjanin says, at paragraph 430, what's required for a finding that a person is a participant in a JCE is that "the criminal purpose," and I'm quoting here, "the criminal purpose is not merely the same but also common to all the persons acting together within a joint criminal enterprise." So it's not enough to say, Well, maybe there is evidence that Mr. Hadzic was involved with some very bad people in OG North. Here we see very bad people also operating in OG South committing the same crimes; therefore, they're in the same JCE. That's not sufficient, Mr. President. It must be the same JCE. It's not just that they are identical common criminal purposes, or that the plans are similar. The common criminal purpose, those who are participants in the crime, who committed these crimes in Lovas, they have to be part of the same criminal plan with Mr. Hadzic. That's the vital point. That's an element, I'd suggest, of what's required to be proven by the Prosecution both as a matter of mens rea and actus reus. Now, what does the evidence show at its highest in respect of the crimes in Lovas village which occur in October, about a month before Vukovar falls? And that's an important fact. The crimes alleged in the indictment, the killings, the minefield incident, occurs a month before Vukovar has fallen. Now, GH-102, who was certainly not the most favourable witness to Mr. Hadzic, said that Mr. Hadzic only visited Lovas after this incident occurred, because GH-102 says that he arrived after the Lovas minefield incident occurred and that he only saw Mr. Hadzic there after that date. So there is no indication of Mr. Hadzic and no evidence in this case of Mr. Hadzic having been in Lovas either contemporaneous with these events or before these events. There is no indication of that. No evidence of that. Ljuban Devetak, what's his connection potentially with the structures of the district government? Well, he allegedly, according to one witness, attended the meeting at Velepromet -- and let me just go back and say that the reference to GH-102's testimony is at paragraph 150 of his 92 ter statement which I will provide a reference for shortly. Ljuban Devetak, according to GH-028, at transcript page 6420, allegedly attends the meeting at Velepromet on the 20th of November. But there is no evidence as to what he was doing there, why he was there, who he spoke to, whether he spoke with Mr. Hadzic, whether he had any position at all in the authorities of this district government. And Your Honours know, you've heard evidence that there were - and this is from Witness Nielsen, who said that, Yes, there were instances where individuals were walking around appropriating titles for themselves, positions representing that they had certain authority when, in fact, there was no foundation for that. The witness's indication that Ljuban Devetak is merely present more than a month after the minefield incident at a meeting in a room where Mr. Hadzic is also present is in no way probative of an indication that Mr. Hadzic has any responsibility, knowledge, or contributed to that crime in Lovas. GH-027, now he said: "... when operations were over in Vukovar ... they," and I'll say "they," it's a reference to the civilian authorities at large or generally, he wasn't very specific, anyway, "they," because here we're looking at the evidence in its highest, "... they established some town commands of their own," and then he refers to Devetak. And that's GH-027 at transcript page 7956. Again, this is after the fall of Vukovar, more than a month after the minefield event and long after the abuses or the unlawful detentions that are described in the indictment. At transcript page 2831, GH-024 says that Bogic met Devetak at some unspecified date, and GH-024 also says that he did not know whether Mr. Hadzic was aware of the Lovas minefield incident. Now, even assuming that there is some potential association between Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Bogic, there is no indication that Mr. Bogic shared any information about this incident, much less that Bogic was the conduit for conveying any instructions that would have contributed to this crime. There is no indication of that whatsoever. And even if you were not to close the door on that and say, Well, this is just the 98 bis stage, even if you were to say that, there is no indication as to when this meeting occurs. No suggestion in the evidence that it occurs contemporaneous with or before the crimes alleged in the indictment. And we say that that's a precondition for finding liability on this ground -- for this crime. It says there on the slide that GH-012 makes that statement -- that might be GH-102, and I'm come back to Your Honours to verify the accuracy of that reference. But in any event, I do believe it was at P50, paragraph 149. He did not learn of the incident until later, after the event occurred. And that's someone who would have been in a position similar to Mr. Hadzic in terms of knowledge of these events in OG South, which, again, at this time is physically cut off from OG north. Velepromet, Mr. President. The allegations are set out in paragraph 31 and 41 -- 41(j) and paragraph 39 of the indictment. The essence of the crimes at Velepromet is that interrogations were conducted there in the course of which individuals were beaten, insulted, or otherwise mistreated. At least 17 were shot dead at Velepromet. And that's on or about the 19th of November. The evidence heard in the case suggested it was in the days preceding, leading up to the 19th, and the 19th, but certainly didn't occur after noon on the 20th of 1991. Now, what's the evidence about who is at Velepromet during these events? Well, the evidence was that the Vukovar TO is still subordinated to the JNA as of the -- up until at least the 21st of November, 1991. We say beyond. But there can't be any doubt that at least up until the 21st of November they were still subordinated to the JNA, and that's P1995.1981, in which we see orders being issued to them, and Theunens confirmed that at transcript page 4561. Very shortly before these events, the commander of the TO Vukovar, as he's described, Vujovic, is appointed by Mrksic or Sljivancanin. The only debate, apparently, appears to be which of the two appointed him, whether it was Mrksic or Sljivancanin. And the sources for that can be found in Jaksic's testimony at 7072 to 7073 and Theunens's testimony at 4561. To the extent it's relevant, it's also clear from P1995.1981, that Leva Supoderica, that unit, is also subordinated to the JNA up until at least the 21st of November, 1991. The evidence at transcript page 8960 was that JNA soldiers were bringing detainees to Velepromet during those days. GH-063 at transcript page 8674: "JNA military police was in charge of guarding us." Military police were present upon the arrival of prisoners, that's P3000, which is a 92 ter statement with a transcript, and the transcript page is 6359. Those military police or other JNA soldiers or reservists were present at Velepromet, we say, fully in control of Velepromet throughout those days. And to the extent that there were TO individuals there, they were subordinated to the JNA. That was their headquarters. And it was the headquarters of the man who had been appointed by Mrksic and/or Sljivancanin. Of course there were rabble who came in there, but if a rabble came in there and committed crimes, a facility like that, as Your Honours have seen, that was with, at the very least, the acquiescence of the JNA and those under its authority and subordinated to it. All of the crimes, at least according to the evidence, happened before that meeting that occurred at Velepromet sometimes on the 20th of November, and there is no evidence of Mr. Hadzic being at Velepromet before that time or having any knowledge of what's going on there. And it's not just that. There is no indication that he has any effective control, no organisational power over anyone who's in Velepromet committing those crimes. And that's the essence of it, Mr. President. There has to be that evidence somewhere. There has to be evidence that he knows -- starting with knowledge, there has to be knowledge that these crimes are taking place or will take place. He has to have at least an awareness that that's going to occur, and if he doesn't, then there cannot be liability for those crimes. It's really as simple as that. Now, Ovcara. Now, the vast majority of the victims at Ovcara, as the evidence showed, did indeed come from Vukovar hospital. And the allegation in the indictment is that the forces present at Ovcara hangar on the 20th of November beat and tortured the victims for hours, before then transporting them to a remote location towards Grahovo farm where 260 were shot and killed and then interred in a mass grave. And that's appropriately charged not only as extermination and murder but also other crimes including imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment. Now, what's the evidence about how those victims ended up in that mass grave? Well, first of all, the transport to Vukovar hospital was ordered and supervised by Sljivancanin, using JNA and TO forces, as well as volunteers. That's at P1040, paragraph 100. And Your Honours will also remember Dr. Bosanac's testimony about that; in particular, what kind of people were performing this task under Mr. Sljivancanin's direction. At P1981, paragraph 38, and GH-80, transcript page 3334, we know that it was the military police of the JNA who escorted the victims from the hospital to the JNA barracks, and that then it was the JNA military police who escorted those victims as prisoners from the JNA barracks to Ovcara. At P1981, which is GH-110's 92 ter statement, at paragraph 42, we know that there were several dozen TO soldiers present in Ovcara at that time, but the number that he estimated to be there of TO soldiers was 35. The testimony there was that Vujovic, Vujovic, Miroljub Vujovic, the man appointed by Mrksic or Sljivancanin was in command of those TO elements at Ovcara. And there we see the references indicating that. Again, it's Jaksic at transcript page 7072 to -73; Theunens, 4563; Theunens 4561. There were JNA officers at Ovcara during the beatings and inhumane treatment of the victims, including Major Vukasinovic and another unidentified colonel and other members of the Guards Motorised Brigade as well as, yes, civilians and volunteers. And that's at P1981, GH-110, paragraphs 38, 42, and 46. And how did GH-110 sum up the situation at paragraph 47 of P1981: "The presence of the soldiers of the 1st gmtbr in the hangar led me to conclude that the 1st gmtbr was in charge of the operation." And let's remember the context in which this transfer at Ovcara takes place. Thousands of prisoners are being taken in the custody of the JNA in what can only be described as a massive operation from Vukovar to Serbia. They have got custody of them. That's what they are doing. That's their task. They are not handing custody over to others, although they are co-opting those under their control to perform and assist with that massive operation. And Ovcara, in every detail, in every indication, is identical to those other movements in terms of who is doing the guarding, the vehicles that they are transported in, the timing, who is commanding it. There is no difference between that operation in Ovcara and all the other JNA removal operations of prisoners except, regrettably, and tragically, for the fate of the victims. Now, after these beatings during the day on the 20th, how was it that they met their terrible fate? Well, according to GH-080, a reliable and important witness, at least in respect of his account of his transport: The evacuation from the Ovcara hangar after dark on 20 November was supervised by "the man with the whistle," at 3364, who he previously described at 3349, as "a man, stocky, with a mustache, wearing a JNA windcheater with a rank insignia and a whistle, and with that whistle he somehow supervised those people." Pressed on the issue of the vehicle -- by the Prosecution, pressed on the issue of the kind of vehicle he was transported in from the Ovcara hangar to the mass grave -- towards the mass grave, he insisted it was "undoubtedly a military vehicle." And he was asked more than once about that. And that he was transferred -- and that the people driving that vehicle were soldiers. And a further indication: "Q. ... did you see JNA members with white belts? "A. I believe that those people took us from the hangar, but I'm not sure at this moment." Now, what is the evidence of Mr. Hadzic's connection with this event? What evidence is there of his knowledge that this event was going to occur? What basis is there for saying that Mr. Hadzic would know that this particular group would be diverted from the course of all the other prisoners who were sent to Serbia? What basis of knowledge is there for him to know that they are going to be diverted from that, sent to Ovcara, beaten, abused, and killed? There is no basis, Mr. President. There is no basis to suggest that he knew that that was going to happen. Now, the Prosecution, of course, is going to rely on the statements made in Sid and the tenor of the government's meeting in Velepromet which, yes, occurs at roughly overlapping time-periods, let's say, and timing is an issue in this case, so I -- but I'm not going to make any specific submissions on that, but the mere fact that there is a meeting going on in which there is a discussion as to how alleged war criminals should be tried, amongst those prisoners, by whom they should be tried, and where, is not evidence that goes to his knowledge of a massacre that day. And this goes back to the submission I made at the beginning about circumstantial evidence. Yes, in a -- on the most bare bones definition of circumstantial evidence, is that circumstantial evidence? It can't be gainsay, Mr. President, because the definition of circumstantial evidence is so open jawed and flexible, and there is nothing wrong with that. But at the 98 bis stage, it's not just whether there is some evidence that's out there that can be classified as circumstantial evidence; therefore, you get over the 98 bis hurdle. I think Your Honours should feel free and open to analyse whether, even viewed in conjunction of all the other evidence, there is any possibility that you could exclude the possibility that Mr. Hadzic -- a reasonable possibility that Mr. Hadzic doesn't know that that event is going to occur. And if there is no evidence on which you can foresee that possibility, then you should not allow this charge to go forward. You should enter a judgement of acquittal in respect of Ovcara. Not only is that a matter that would be efficient, not only would it accelerate proceedings and relieve the Defence of the opportunity to bring evidence in respect of a charge that is manifestly -- an account that is manifestly unproven, it also assures that a man charged with a crime, for which there is no credible basis, does not have to suffer under the cloud of that charge any longer. And I suggest that Your Honours have more than adequate discretion to look at that evidence and determine whether you see any path going forward for a conviction for the events at Ovcara. Opatovac. Now at paragraph 41(k), the crimes of imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, and cruel treatment are alleged in respect of various forces allegedly engaging in those crimes in the police station in Opatovac. And the evidence has come up there in a single block. And the evidence about who the perpetrators are and what they do is, in a broad view of things, as follows: The initial assault on Opatovac leads to "Serbian reservists entering the village together with the JNA," and those who do the initial beatings and detaining at the Dom Kultura have "a white belt." That's GH-085 at transcript page 8537 and 8538. The individuals running the TO, according to Witness GH-061, at 8623, are from Belgrade because of their accent. They are not locals. They are from Belgrade. And those are the individuals who are in residence occupying the local commune office. GH-061, who sought a travel pass to leave Opatovac at a certain time, as described at 8633 to 8634, observed that it was the JNA military police who, on that occasion, instructed those local TO personnel to issue the pass. And then, finally, we come back to the quotation from Mr. Theunens in respect of the document in December by Mr. Belic, Colonel Belic, saying that there are no civilian authorities in place in Opatovac in early December, which means by default that it's the JNA town commands that are in control of civilian affairs in Opatovac. That's the Prosecution's own witness, Mr. President. Now, we say, again, coming back to what I called earlier the cardinal elements of the modes of liability charged in respect of the specific incidents of abuse or mistreatment or detention in Opatovac, where is the evidence that Mr. Hadzic intended those crimes? Where is the evidence that those crimes were encompassed by a joint criminal enterprise of which he is a member? It doesn't come through the organisational structure, Mr. President. That evidence isn't there. There is no connection between Mr. Hadzic's office as president of the district government and the people who were committing these crimes or the people who are criminally liable for these crimes. The evidence not only is devoid of that, it shows what the organisational structure is. And this is all Prosecution evidence, Mr. President. These are all Prosecution witnesses who provided this evidence about what structures were in place, who was doing what. And I suggest to you that it's not enough to rely on abstractions and speculation about, for example, the place that the JNA may play -- the role the JNA may play in some, what I suggest is an entirely unsubstantiated JCE emanating from Mr. Milosevic. Because at the end of the day isn't that the panacea JCE that could be relied on, to say, Well, these are all moving components of a vast JCE whose purpose is to bring about Greater Serbia? Well, again, Mr. President, I take you back to the 98 bis standard of circumstantial evidence. It's simply not enough, in my submission, that there be jots of evidence about Greater Serbia or jots of evidence about the role of the president or jots of evidence as to how President Milosevic might be at the pinnacle of some overarching structure or scheme that somehow connects Mr. Hadzic with these individual crimes in Opatovac. If the evidence is there, and if it's enough for you to say, Well, at the end of the day, there is sufficient evidence here to exclude the reasonable possibility that Mr. Hadzic doesn't know about that, then allow the charges to proceed. You can do that. But I say you also have a discretion to say this evidence, even taken at its highest, isn't going to be able to exclude that possibility. Crimes in Serbia. Counts 5 to 9 of the indictment, when read in conjunction with paragraphs 41(a) to (d), allege certain crimes as having taken place in Serbia. And the question is -- the question raised by that is: On what basis is international humanitarian law, the law of armed conflict, extended to the territory of Serbia, and, equally, by what -- on what basis or on what theory are crimes alleged under Article 5, which must be in armed conflict, to -- on what basis are they extended to the territory of Serbia? Now the question arises because based on a -- what I would suggest is a conventional view of the law of internal armed conflict, the principle is that liability and the scope of IHL extends to crimes committed in the territory of the country where that armed conflict is taking place, if that conflict is characterised as internal. And here we have a quotation from the Tadic jurisdiction decision of the 2nd October, 1995. And admittedly, Your Honours, it's addressed to a different issue. It's coming at it from the other point of view. It's inquiring whether or not crimes need to be committed on the battlefield in order to fall within the scope of IHL, or can it be committed further away from the battlefield and still be subject to that body of law. But in answering that and addressing that issue, the Appeals Chamber said: "... we find that an armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between States or protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups within a State. International humanitarian law applies from the initiation of such armed conflicts and extends beyond the cessation of hostilities until a general conclusion of peace is reached; or, in the case of internal conflicts, a peaceful settlement is achieved. Until that moment, international humanitarian law continues to apply in the whole territory of the warring States or, in the case of internal conflicts, the whole territory under the control of a party, whether or not actual combat takes place that." Now it's not our position, and I don't want Your Honours to believe it's our position, that international humanitarian law cannot extend beyond necessarily -- cannot necessarily extend beyond the territory of a state where an internal armed conflict is taking place. It is possible to have spillover, and that is recognised in the doctrine. But if there is spillover, Mr. President and Your Honours, then it must be shown that there is an armed conflict that extends outside of that territory. There must be proof that the armed conflict indeed does spill over. If it doesn't spill over and if there isn't evidence of that spillover, then we suggest that the Tadic statement is the default principle and the default rule, that in an internal armed conflict, the skoal scope of IHL extends only to the territory of the state where that armed conflict is taking place. Now just as an aside, Mr. President, it's noteworthy that there is no characterisation of the armed conflict in the indictment, and I didn't hear a characterisation during the opening statement, and I haven't heard a characterisation taken throughout the Prosecution case. And there is a statement from the Hadzihasanovic case, from the 21st of February, 2003, from the Appeals Chamber, paragraph 12, it's decision pursuant to Rule 72(E) as to validity of appeal, and one of the interesting statements in this decision is that following the withdrawal of both the Article 2 charges -- and let me just stop there. Article 2, of course, concerns grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, and that applies only in international armed conflicts, and let's be clear that it's not charged in this case, so I'm not -- there is no issue of Article 2 in this case as such. And that's not why the quotation is relevant. Following the withdrawal of both the Article 2 charges and the express allegation in the original indictment that the armed conflict was international in character, the prosecution should not be permitted to rely upon the imprecision of its current pleading in order to put forward a case that the armed conflicted was international in character without a further amendment to its indictment to make this expressly clear. So the position that seems to be set out in that decision, which may or may not derive from the fact that Article 2 charges were dropped previously from the indictment, but leaving aside that potential explanation, the principle that seems to flow from this statement is that where an armed conflict is not characterised in an indictment, that the presumption is it's an internal armed conflict. That's what this decision appears to be saying. So on what basis is the Prosecution contending that IHL extends to Serbia? And there is a lot of moving parts here, Mr. President. First of all, we say it's not enough to just say, Well, there is evidence of an armed conflict. That's not enough. There has to be evidence that explains either how the internal armed conflict has expanded to encompass the territories of an adjacent state, or to indicate how the elements for an international armed conflict are satisfied, and to argue that that is indeed the characterisation of the conflict being proffered. Now, I don't know if that is the characterisation of the conflict being proffered, and there may be evidence to sustain it, but the Prosecution has an obligation, even at the 98 bis stage, to indicate what evidence it is relying on to assert either that there is a spillover of an internal armed conflict, or that the conditions for establishing an international armed conflict exist. And amongst the elements that would have to be shown, at least as relevant to this case, is that Croatia is a state at the relevant times. And the Prosecution would have to establish that element, that Croatia is a state, for the purposes of determining the application and the characterisation of the conflict. And just to graphically represent this issue, Mr. President. If it's an internal armed conflict, the scope of application, presumptively, is Croatia. If the conflict is international between Serbia and Croatia, then the scope of application would be as represented on the screen, extending to the entire territory of Serbia. And by the way, that's also particularly relevant, Mr. President, because at least one of the detention facilities is very, very far away from the border, hundreds of kilometres. So it's not just a theoretical thing to ask how exactly does the armed conflict extend the scope of international humanitarian law to abuses, because that's what's charged in the indictment, to abuses that occur at a prison hundreds of miles, not just from the theater of conflict, hundreds of miles from the state in which the internal armed conflict is taking place. What's the element? What is the evidence that is being relied on to support a characterisation of the conflict which extends international humanitarian law to such a prison? And I'll suggest a third option, of course: Let's say that Croatia is not a state at the relevant times, maybe the Prosecution's view is that there is an internal armed conflict in the SFRY, in which case IHL would apply throughout the territory, according to the learning of Tadic, of the former SFRY, as it now is known. Mr. President, I see the break is upon us, and I've completed my submissions. Again, to recap: This is a broad case with a broad scope with 14 charges, two and a half years, the entire territory that at any time was autonomous from Croatia in 1991 to 1993. And it's a circumstantial case. We have not challenged at the 98 bis stage every single crime. We have not challenged every single event that could be characterised as a count. We have challenged what we believe as genuinely not been the product or shown to be provable based on the evidence presented in this case. And part of that, Mr. President, is because this is fundamentally a circumstantial case, a case that is based upon a conjunction of factors. And if Your Honours, based on a review of the conjunction of factors that we've set out in respect of the specific crimes that we have identified, find that there is no path to conviction, then you may acquit. You may acquit on those specific charges, on those specific counts, and that's what we ask you to do. Thank you, Your Honours.
